# Labour Party Manifesto 2015: Summary

## Britain Can Be Better

The 2015 Labour Manifesto presents a vision of national renewal centred on the principle that **Britain only succeeds when working people succeed**. The document opens with a "Budget Responsibility Lock" – a commitment that every policy is fully funded without additional borrowing, the deficit will be cut every year, and national debt will fall during the parliament.

## Economic Vision

Labour argues the economy has fundamentally failed working families. The link between national prosperity and household finances has been broken, with wages falling by £1,600 annually since 2010 – the greatest decline since 1874. Over five million people earn below the Living Wage, while zero-hours contracts and food bank usage have soared.

The manifesto positions Labour as both **pro-business and pro-worker**, rejecting the Conservative view that success depends only on those at the top. Key economic pledges include raising the minimum wage to £8 by 2019, banning exploitative zero-hours contracts, introducing a British Investment Bank, cutting business rates for small firms, and restoring the 50p tax rate for incomes over £150,000 while abolishing non-dom status.

## Public Services

The NHS represents Labour's proudest achievement, yet faces existential threat under Conservative values. Labour pledges £2.5 billion additional investment for 20,000 nurses, 8,000 GPs and 3,000 midwives, funded by a Mansion Tax on properties over £2 million. The manifesto promises to repeal the Health and Social Care Act, end privatisation, and create an integrated service joining physical health, mental health and social care.

On education, Labour commits to protecting the entire budget, guaranteeing qualified teachers, capping infant class sizes, and creating gold-standard Technical Baccalaureates for vocational routes.

## Families and Communities

Labour offers expanded free childcare (25 hours for working parents), doubled paternity leave, and a commitment to build 200,000 homes annually. The cruel Bedroom Tax will be abolished, and renters guaranteed three-year tenancies with rent rise ceilings.

On immigration, Labour acknowledges public anxiety whilst rejecting isolation. Migrants will wait two years before claiming benefits, with stronger border controls and laws preventing wage undercutting through worker exploitation.

## Constitutional Reform

The manifesto proposes the biggest devolution in a century through an English Devolution Act transferring £30 billion to city and county regions. Labour commits to replacing the House of Lords with an elected Senate, votes at 16, and implementing the Smith Agreement for Scotland.

## International Outlook

Labour presents itself as internationalist, committed to EU membership while pursuing reform. The manifesto emphasises NATO commitment, maintenance of the nuclear deterrent, and climate leadership pushing for net-zero global emissions by century's end.

## Conclusion

The manifesto frames a clear choice: continue with an economy serving only privileged elites, or change direction together. Labour's plan promises to rebuild Britain so that working people finally share in prosperity, with everyone playing by the same rules – including those at the top.
